processing: In one account from a Bulang village, the leaf is cooked for around ten minutes, drained, packed into a section of bamboo, sealed with red clay and buried for six months to two years, with the tube watered underground.
harvest_season: Not well documented; picking time and leaf standard vary by household.
appearance_dry: Not a dry tea in the usual sense: a dense, moist mass of dark, soft fermented leaf, as is typical of pickled teas.
appearance_liquor: Little is documented about an infusion, since it is mainly eaten; expect a pale, dull amber if it is steeped, as with other fermented leaf.
appearance_wet: Soft, dark olive-brown leaves that have lost their spring and hold together in clumps.
taste_profile: Sour but clean, in the one account that describes tasting leaf buried over a year; detailed tasting notes for this tea are scarce.

brewing.notes: Normally chewed or eaten as a food rather than brewed. If you steep a pinch, treat it as an experiment; there is no established brewing method.

vintage_note: Made in small household batches and rarely sold as a graded commercial tea, so there are no recognised vintages or seasons on the market. A batch is ready after its time underground and is usually eaten locally.
description:
Bulang sour tea is less a drink than a food: tea leaf pickled by the Bulang people of southern Yunnan and eaten. It belongs to the same family as the pickled teas of Southeast Asia, and it has little to do with what you would normally put in a gaiwan.

The method is simple and slow. In a village near Menghai the leaf is cooked, drained, packed into bamboo, sealed with red clay and buried for six months to two years.

The point is a clean sourness. Few detailed tasting descriptions exist, and most accounts focus on how it is made rather than how each batch differs, so approach it without fixed expectations.

You are unlikely to find it in a tea shop. If you meet it, it will probably be homemade, in a Bulang village around Menghai, and that is the best way to try it. Do not confuse it with the sour tea of the De'ang people, a separate tradition with its own national heritage listing.
history: Little is firmly documented, and no reliable dating of the practice is available. A travel account from Nongyang, a mainly Bulang village about half an hour from Menghai, records it as a living local food, eaten plain or with salt, garlic and chilli, and served at weddings and celebrations.
